findings.title: The embedded-post author link reverses its intended lightness levels
findings.body: This selector previously used `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`, but the light-theme branch is now 70% and the dark-theme branch is 30%. This both changes the established light-theme appearance and gives dark themes the inverse of the intended secondary-derived contrast. It should retain the 30% primary branch and use the corresponding 70% secondary branch.

findings.title: Group member names lose their intended lighter-theme emphasis
findings.body: The `.group-member-info .name` rule previously used `$primary` at 30% lightness, but the new expression uses 50% for both branches. As a result, light themes no longer preserve the existing name color and dark themes do not get the corresponding `$secondary` 70% value. Use primary 30% and secondary 70%, as is already done for comparable user names.

findings.title: The custom-message length hint has its contrast levels inverted
findings.body: This hint was previously `$primary` at 70% lightness, but the change replaces it with primary 30% and secondary 70%. That makes the hint substantially darker on light themes and much brighter on dark themes instead of preserving its de-emphasized appearance. The branches should be primary 70% and secondary 30%.

findings.title: Mobile topic-map headings no longer retain their original contrast
findings.body: The topic-map `h3` color was `$primary` at 20% lightness, but it was changed to 50% for both theme branches. This weakens the heading on light themes and fails to use the corresponding high-lightness secondary value needed for dark backgrounds. Preserve the 20% primary branch and use secondary at 80% for dark themes.

findings.title: Mobile group member names use the wrong lightness pair
findings.body: The mobile `.group-member-info .name` rule had primary lightness 30%, but the new code changes it to 50% and pairs it with secondary 50%. This changes the light-theme hierarchy and does not provide the expected secondary 70% dark-theme counterpart. The rule should use primary 30% and secondary 70%, matching the intended name styling.
